claims.text: The native iron-oxide layer on pre-exposure Q235 steel acts as a protective corrosion barrier at room temperature.
In salt-rich environments at 700–900 °C, the native oxide layer on Q235 steel becomes susceptible to degradation.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and Q235 steel substrate causes microcracking and spallation of the oxide at high temperature.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel carries a native, as-formed iron-oxide film.
The native film is likely a mixture of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
The integrity and adhesion of the native iron-oxide layer govern its corrosion protection.
At room temperature, the native oxide remains cohesive and limits corrosive attack by the salt deposit.
Oxide cracking and spallation expose fresh Q235 steel to the salt environment, accelerating corrosion and degradation.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, salt-exposed samples at 700–900 °C will show greater mass change, a higher surface-microcrack density, and visible oxide spallation.
Room-temperature salt-exposed samples will retain a comparatively intact oxide layer and exhibit minimal corrosion.
At lower temperature or in the absence of salt deposits, the native oxide should remain protective and the predicted degradation should not occur.
Mass change can be used as an indicator of oxidation and corrosion progression in this experiment.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes oxide failure to temperature-driven expansion mismatch, which can occur during high-temperature exposure without salt, whereas the boundary states that absence of salt should prevent the predicted degradation and implies that removing salt lowers thermal stress. The proposed mechanism does not explain why salt absence would remove expansion-mismatch stress.
